source.title: SWE-Mirror: Scaling Issue-Resolving Datasets by Mirroring Issues Across Repositories
source.authors: Jun-Hao Wang; Dao-Guang Zan; Shu-Lin Xin; Si-Yao Liu; Yurong Wu; Kai Shen

record.tranche_reason: The study varies the amount of post-training data and measures downstream issue-resolution performance, bearing on the claim that downstream performance improves with scale. It does not measure pretraining loss or the original language-model scaling quantities.
record.gate_note: The data-scale ablation in Section 3.3.1 reports downstream resolve rates as training trajectory count varies. Dataset statistics, filter and mirroring success rates, cross-lingual results, and benchmark comparisons that do not vary scale are not separate results on the tested version.
record.test_reason: This is a dataset paper. Its 'scaling' result is a fine-tuning ablation: 512 to 4096 agent trajectories, three loss-masking strategies, 7B and 32B models, scored by SWE-Bench-Verified resolve rate. It borrows Kaplan's scaling-law label to show its dataset's value. It fits no power law, makes no prediction, and does not vary pretraining parameters, tokens or compute. V6 concerns downstream performance as a function of model scale or pretraining loss, so it does not match. V5's fine-tuning clause needs the power-law form, which is never tested. The result belongs under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors claim a 'strong scaling law' in which resolve rate consistently improves with training-data volume. That claim rests on SFT trajectory counts, with no fitted law. They also conclude that Error Masking beats the other strategies by a gap that widens with data, and that non-Python training data transfers to Python tasks.
record.recipe_differences: This is post-training on issue-resolving agent trajectories with SWE-Bench-Verified resolve rate as the outcome, rather than scaling language-model pretraining and measuring held-out cross-entropy loss.
record.method_sensitivity: Training strategy (Error Prune, Response Only, Error Masking) and model size (7B, 32B) are varied; the authors say the data-scale improvement is consistent across these settings.

fits_no_version.finding: SWE-Bench-Verified resolve rate rises with the number of SFT trajectories (512–4096) for the 7B and 32B models under three loss-masking strategies. The authors say the gain is consistent; the 32B Error Mask model reaches 35.6% at 4096, from an untuned 6.2%. No functional form is fitted.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream agentic task performance increases monotonically with fine-tuning data quantity (fine-tuning data scaling of downstream performance).

record.problems: For most plotted conditions, the extracted figure text does not permit reliable assignment of individual values; the prose gives one explicit numerical endpoint comparison. No uncertainty estimates are reported. The scale result is for one downstream benchmark and post-training trajectory counts, not pretraining loss or a fitted power law.
record.rows_left_out: No additional relevant data-scale results were omitted. The extracted Figure 2 values beyond the explicit 32B Error Masking endpoint were not assigned to conditions because the flattened figure text does not establish those associations.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss vs parameters, tokens or compute.
No fitted law and no extrapolation.
Fine-tuning data is varied, but no power-law form is fitted or tested. There are only four data sizes.
Model size is varied only as 7B vs 32B base models. Downstream predictability from pretraining scale or loss is not examined.
No exponent fitting or fitting-choice comparison.

record.verdict_notes: The ablation trains runs under 4k trajectories with a different learning rate (1e-4, 5 epochs) and context setup than the main models, so the Table 6 results on 12,456 trajectories (22.8%/52.2%) are not on the same curve. No uncertainty is reported. Each curve has only four points.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss scaling with parameter count, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger runs from power laws fitted on small runs.
Effects of architecture shape at fixed parameter count.
Power laws in other modalities or training regimes such as repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer.

The study varies post-training trajectory count and evaluates SWE-Bench-Verified resolve rate; it does not test pretraining loss, model-size scaling, or downstream performance across other tasks as a function of these quantities.
Dependence of exponents or compute-optimal splits on fitting choices, setup, or curve bending.

rows.subject: SWE-Mirror-LM-32B
rows.operation_detail: Train with increasing trajectory counts using Error Masking and measure SWE-Bench-Verified resolve rate.
rows.note: The authors identify 6.2% as the baseline and report 35.6% after training on 4096 trajectories.
rows.check: The 6.2% baseline is the untuned Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct (Table 6), not the 512-trajectory point. The 6.2→35.6 gain therefore mixes fine-tuning itself with the data-scale effect. The condition is mislabelled 'Error Masking' at 4096 only, so the row is not a scaling curve. There is no power-law fit.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: SWE-Bench-Verified resolve rate for the tested 7B and 32B models across 512–4096 training trajectories and the three reported training strategies
reader_labels.reason: The authors state that performance consistently improves with more training data across both model sizes and all strategies; R1–R6 record this result, including the explicit 32B Error Masking increase in R6.
